title: Ninety-Seven Miles: the Boss, the Ice, and the Boat That Went for Help
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Kilkea to Dulwich: A Doctor's Son Goes to Sea

stops.name: Kilkea House, County Kildare: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates are those of Kilkea village; the house itself has no separately confirmed fix.
stops.campa: Ernest Henry Shackleton is born at Kilkea House, near the village of Kilkea in County Kildare, second of the ten children of Henry Shackleton and Henrietta Gavan. The family are Quaker-descended tenant farmers on Anglo-Irish land, and the house stands among tillage fields a few miles from Athy. The father will not stay a farmer. Within six years he gives up the land, enters Trinity College Dublin to read medicine, and moves the household to the city. Ernest is six years old when they go.
suggested_refs: The Shackleton Museum at Athy, County Kildare, the only permanent Shackleton exhibition, a few miles from the birthplace

stops.name: Sydenham, South London: the doctor's practice
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1884; the month and day of the move are not recorded, and the date defaults to 1 January. The intervening Dublin years (from 1880, at an address given in the dossier as 35 Marlborough Road) are attested only to the city, not to the street.
stops.campa: Henry Shackleton moves his wife, his son, and eight daughters from Dublin to Sydenham in south London and sets up a doctor's practice. Ernest is ten, Irish in an English suburb, the only boy in a house full of sisters, with a father who expects him to follow into medicine. He does not. He reads sea stories and asks about ships instead, and the family argues about it for months. The Royal Navy wants money and influence the Shackletons have not got. The argument settles on the merchant marine, which wants neither. He will be sent to sea at sixteen.

stops.name: Dulwich College: the unremarkable schoolboy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1887-1890; the year of entry is given differently across sources and no day is recorded, so the date defaults to 1 January 1887.
stops.campa: He enters Dulwich College as a day boy and leaves no mark on its prize lists. Masters find him unremarkable; he is bored by the classroom and reads Keats and Browning on his own account, verse he will recite years later to men lying in sleeping bags on the Ross Ice Shelf. He is sixteen when he goes. The twenty-three-foot lifeboat James Caird, which will carry six men eight hundred miles of Southern Ocean in 1916, is given to the college in 1922 and stands there now. It went out once, to the National Maritime Museum, for conservation between 1967 and 1985.
suggested_refs: The James Caird, on display at Dulwich College since 1922, donated by John Quiller Rowett; conserved at the National Maritime Museum 1967-1985

stops.name: Liverpool: apprenticed to the Hoghton Tower
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1890; the sailing month is not fixed in reachable sources and the date defaults to 1 January. Liverpool is the North Western Shipping Company's home port; the specific berth is not recorded.
stops.campa: At sixteen he signs with the North Western Shipping Company and goes to sea in the Hoghton Tower, a full-rigged sailing ship on the long southern runs. The apprenticeship is the hard school: watches in the dark, ice in the rigging, the forecastle's settled opinion of a doctor's son from London. He passes for second mate in August 1894 and takes his first mate's certificate in 1896. The Board of Trade certifies him master in 1898. He is twenty-four.
suggested_refs: Board of Trade certificates of competency, second mate 1894, first mate 1896, master 1898
sources: Dulwich College archives, certification record (via dossier)

stops.name: Table Bay, Cape Town: the troopship and the patron's son
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1900; the exact voyage dates of the Tintagel Castle are not fixed in reachable sources and the date defaults to 1 January. The Longstaff meeting is standard in the biographies (Huntford; Fisher and Fisher) rather than documented from a ship's paper.
stops.campa: Shackleton is serving the Union-Castle Line's South African run when the Boer War turns the mail boats into troopships. Aboard Tintagel Castle he helps carry twelve hundred soldiers to the Cape, and among the officers he meets Cedric Longstaff, whose father Llewellyn Longstaff is the principal private backer of a national Antarctic expedition then being fitted out in London. Shackleton asks the son for an introduction to the father, and the introduction is made. No ship's paper or letter recording the meeting has been found; it reaches the record through Huntford and through Fisher and Fisher, and rests on the biographies alone.

segments.name: Discovery: Third Officer, and Sent Home

stops.name: East India Docks, London: Discovery sails south
stops.date_confidence: attested. The appointment as third officer was confirmed 17 February 1901 and the Royal Naval Reserve commission dated 4 June 1901; both are folded into this stop.
stops.campa: Appointed third officer of the British National Antarctic Expedition in February and commissioned sub-lieutenant in the Royal Naval Reserve in June, Shackleton takes Discovery down the Thames on the last day of July under Robert Falcon Scott. He is twenty-seven and has never seen ice. His duties are the holds, the stores, the seawater analysis and the ship's entertainments; he edits the winter magazine and runs the theatricals. The voyage calls at Madeira, Cape Town and Lyttelton, and reaches the Antarctic on 9 January 1902.

stops.name: Lyttelton Harbour: the last inhabited coast
stops.date_confidence: the call is attested as Discovery's last major port before the ice; the precise date is not fixed in reachable sources and defaults to 1 November 1901.
stops.campa: Discovery lies at Lyttelton taking on coal, sheep and dogs, the last town before a year and a half of ice. New Zealand sends her off with crowds along the wharf and a sailor falling from the rigging into the water. Shackleton will come back to this same harbour seven years later as a commander in his own right, with his own money at stake. For now he is the third officer, popular in the wardroom, the man the lower deck likes best, watching the last hills of an inhabited country go down astern.

stops.name: Hut Point, McMurdo Sound: the first winter
stops.date_confidence: the winter quarters at Hut Point are attested; the exact date of Discovery's arrival is given variously and this stop is set to February 1902. Coordinates corrected from a fix whose latitude sign placed the stop in the Arctic Ocean.
stops.campa: Discovery is frozen in at Hut Point for the winter, her own hull the expedition's house. The men learn Antarctica by making every error available to them: dogs badly driven, sledges badly packed, scurvy misunderstood, a seaman killed on an ice slope in a blizzard. Shackleton runs the South Polar Times off a printing press set up in the wardroom. In November he is chosen with Scott and the doctor Edward Wilson for the great southern journey. Three men, nineteen dogs, and a ration calculated wrong: they leave on 2 November 1902.
suggested_refs: The South Polar Times, edited by Shackleton at Hut Point, 1902

stops.name: Ross Ice Shelf, 82 degrees 17 minutes south: the record
stops.date_confidence: the Farthest South of the Discovery southern journey is attested to 30 December 1902 (Wikipedia, 'Discovery Expedition'); some chronologies give 14 January 1903, a date that belongs to the return march, and the contradiction is left standing. Longitude is approximate: the party turned near Cape Wilson, 82 degrees 15 minutes south, 164 degrees east. Modern correlation of Shackleton's photograph with Wilson's drawing places the final camp nearer 82 degrees 06 minutes south.
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of December, two months out from the ship, Scott, Wilson and Shackleton stand further south than any human being has stood, roughly 82 degrees 17 minutes on the Ross Ice Shelf with the Victoria Land mountains on their right hand. The dogs are dying and being fed to one another. The return is worse than the outward march: all three are scurvied, Shackleton coughs blood, breaks down, and at times is carried by the party rather than hauling with it. They regain Discovery on 3 February 1903.
suggested_refs: Shackleton's photograph and Edward Wilson's drawing of the turning point, used by later surveyors to recompute the position

stops.name: McMurdo Sound: invalided home on the Morning
stops.date_confidence: that Scott sent Shackleton home on the relief ship early in 1903 is attested from Scott's own account; the exact date of Morning's departure is given variously in reachable sources and is set here to early March 1903.
stops.campa: Scott orders Shackleton home on the relief ship Morning as an invalid, judged unfit for a second winter. The two men's accounts of the decision never quite agree, and the historiography has argued about it for a century: a commander's medical prudence, or the removal of a subordinate who had proved more popular than his captain. He is twenty-nine years old and has been in Antarctica for fourteen months. Shackleton weeps on the deck as Morning pulls away.
sources: Robert Falcon Scott, The Voyage of the Discovery (1905)

segments.name: Edinburgh, Westminster, Dundee: The Years Ashore

stops.name: Edinburgh: secretary of the Royal Scottish Geographical Society
stops.date_confidence: the appointment date and the resignation of 10 November 1905 are attested; the coordinates are an approximate central Edinburgh placement, the Society's period address not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: He takes the secretaryship of the Royal Scottish Geographical Society at a salary and holds it not quite two years. The work is committee minutes, membership drives, lecture bookings, and he is good at it in the way he is good at anything that involves persuading people in a room. What he is actually doing in Edinburgh is building a list: shipowners, industrialists, newspaper men, the kind of subscriber who might one day pay for a ship. He resigns on 10 November 1905.
sources: Royal Scottish Geographical Society records (via dossier)

stops.name: Christ Church, Westminster: the marriage to Emily Dorman
stops.date_confidence: the marriage date is attested; the church's exact coordinates could not be confirmed and this is an approximate Westminster placement.
stops.campa: Shackleton marries Emily Mary Dorman, six years his senior, whom he has courted since before Discovery. Cyril Longhurst, secretary of the expedition, stands as best man; the wedding breakfast is at the house of Sir Clements Markham, who launched the expedition that made Shackleton's name. Emily will spend most of the marriage waiting for him to come back from somewhere. Three children follow: Raymond in February 1905, Cecily in December 1906, Edward in July 1911.

stops.name: Dundee: fourth of five candidates
stops.date_confidence: the result, 3,865 votes and fourth place, is attested from the 1906 general election returns; the polling day within January 1906 is not specified here and the date defaults to 1 January.
stops.campa: He stands for Dundee as a Liberal Unionist: a polar explorer thrown at a working-class Scottish seat with no political record and a good speaking voice. Behind the campaign is the same calculation as the Edinburgh secretaryship and the string of failing ventures of these years, cigarettes, Hungarian mining stock, a transport scheme for Russia. He needs money and he needs standing, and none of it is producing either. He finishes fourth of five with 3,865 votes.
sources: 1906 UK general election returns for Dundee (via dossier)

stops.name: Lyttelton Harbour: Nimrod towed south
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates corrected from a fix whose latitude sign placed the harbour off northern Japan.
stops.campa: Nimrod leaves Lyttelton on New Year's Day under tow from the steamer Koonya, because she cannot carry coal enough to steam south under her own power. Shackleton has raised the expedition on a guarantee from the Glasgow industrialist William Beardmore, on loans, and on his own promises. Thirty thousand people watch from the harbour heads. The tow runs fourteen hundred miles to the edge of the pack, the longest yet made at sea. He has promised Scott in writing that he will not use McMurdo Sound.

stops.name: Cape Royds, Ross Island: the hut under the volcano
stops.date_confidence: the base was established 3 February 1908. Coordinates corrected from a fix whose latitude sign placed the cape in the Arctic; Wikipedia gives 77.550 south, 166.150 east.
stops.campa: Ice bars the eastern approaches, and Shackleton, unable to reach King Edward VII Land or the Bay of Whales, breaks his promise to Scott and puts his hut at Cape Royds under the smoking cone of Mount Erebus. He is reproached for it for the rest of his life. Through the winter dark the men run a printing press and produce Aurora Australis, bound in packing-case boards, the first book printed in Antarctica, with Shackleton as editor. In March a party of six makes the first ascent of Erebus; Shackleton stays below with the base and the ponies.
suggested_refs: Aurora Australis (Cape Royds, winter 1908), the first book printed in Antarctica
The first ascent of Mount Erebus, March 1908, by Edgeworth David, Douglas Mawson, Alistair Mackay, Jameson Adams, Eric Marshall and Philip Brocklehurst, a summit party that did not include Shackleton

stops.name: Beardmore Glacier: the road onto the plateau
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1908; the discovery and ascent occupied several weeks and the stop is dated to the month, with the day defaulting to the first.
stops.campa: Marching south with Frank Wild, Eric Marshall and Jameson Adams, Shackleton finds the mountain wall does not open, and then, at the last, it does: a glacier a hundred miles long and up to twenty-five wide, climbing from the Barrier to the polar plateau. He names it for William Beardmore, who guaranteed the expedition's overdraft. The last pony, Socks, goes through a crevasse on the ascent and nearly takes Wild with him. The route becomes the standard road to the Pole, and Scott will die on it four years later.

stops.name: Polar plateau, 88 degrees 23 minutes south: the turn
stops.date_confidence: date and latitude are attested; the longitude of the turning point is approximate.
stops.campa: Ninety-seven geographical miles from the Pole, on short rations at eleven thousand feet, Shackleton works out that the food will not carry four men there and back again. He plants the Union Jack the Queen gave him, names the plateau for Edward VII, and turns around. The return is a starving race between depots, with dysentery in all four men and Shackleton giving his own biscuit to Wild on a day he is no better fed himself. Wild writes in his diary that he will never forget it.
stops.quote: When I returned from the Nimrod Expedition on which we had to turn back from our attempt to plant the British flag on the South Pole, being beaten by stress of circumstances within ninety-seven miles of our goal...
stops.quote_source: Ernest Shackleton, South: The Story of Shackleton's Last Expedition 1914-1917 (1919), Preface
suggested_refs: Frank Wild's sledging diary, 31 January 1909, on Shackleton's gift of the biscuit

stops.name: South Magnetic Pole, Victoria Land: the dip needle stands upright
stops.date_confidence: the date and the party are attested. Shackleton is not present: he is on the southern march twelve hundred miles away, and this stop records an achievement of the expedition he commanded and provisioned, not of his own feet. The magnetic pole moves, so the position is the calculated one of 1909 and not a fixed point.
stops.campa: Edgeworth David, Douglas Mawson and Alistair Mackay man-haul more than twelve hundred miles up the coast of Victoria Land and on the sixteenth of January stand where the dip needle points straight down. They raise the flag, take the possession photograph with a string pulled to the shutter, and turn for the coast with barely food enough to reach the pickup. Shackleton, starving on the plateau at the other end of the same expedition, will know nothing of it for weeks. The two parties are twelve hundred miles apart and have no means of speaking to each other.
suggested_refs: Edgeworth David, The Magnetic Pole journey narrative in Shackleton, The Heart of the Antarctic (1909), vol. II

stops.name: Tidebrook, Sussex: the live donkey
stops.date_confidence: Hugh Robert Mill's authorised biography (1923) places the remark on a Sunday walk at Tidebrook in June 1909; the day is not recorded and the date defaults to the first. Huntford prints a different wording from Emily's own record: 'a live donkey is better than a dead lion, isn't it?' The widely circulated proverb form, 'Better a live donkey than a dead lion,' is a later condensation of one or the other. Coordinates are an approximate placement of the hamlet.
stops.campa: Home from the Nimrod expedition, walking with Emily on a Sunday in the Sussex countryside, Shackleton explains the ninety-seven miles to the one person entitled to an explanation. His authorised biographer records one wording of the sentence; Emily's own account, which Huntford prints, runs differently and ends with her answering yes, as far as I am concerned, and the two of them leaving it there. He is received by Edward VII on 10 July and knighted in November. Which of the two wordings he actually used on that walk is not recoverable, and the proverb everyone now quotes, better a live donkey than a dead lion, is later than either.
stops.quote: Anyway, darling, I thought you would like a living donkey better than a dead lion.
stops.quote_source: Shackleton to Emily Shackleton, Tidebrook, June 1909, in Hugh Robert Mill, The Life of Sir Ernest Shackleton (1923)
suggested_refs: Hugh Robert Mill, The Life of Sir Ernest Shackleton (1923), the authorised biography, full text at archive.org (lifeofsirernests00milluoft)
sources: Hugh Robert Mill, The Life of Sir Ernest Shackleton (1923)

stops.name: Plymouth: Endurance clears for the south
stops.date_confidence: attested. The ship had left London earlier and called at Margate before Plymouth; chronologies that give East India Docks for this departure are conflating it with Discovery's in 1901. Shackleton is not aboard: he follows on 27 September and joins her at Buenos Aires.
stops.campa: Endurance, built at the Framnaes yard in Sandefjord as the polar-cruise ship Polaris and bought and renamed by Shackleton for the family motto Fortitudine vincimus, clears Plymouth four days after Britain declares war on Germany. Shackleton has telegraphed the Admiralty offering ship, stores and men for national service, and Churchill's answer is one word, proceed. He is not aboard. He stays behind chasing the last of the money, meaning to cross the continent from the Weddell Sea to the Ross Sea in a hundred days.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the letter about the ship
stops.date_confidence: the port call is attested to October 1914; the stop is dated to the letter of 26 October 1914 held at the Scott Polar Research Institute, MS 1537/2/31/6;D. The letter has been miscited as written in England before departure; the manuscript places it in Buenos Aires.
stops.campa: Shackleton joins his ship at Buenos Aires, sacks the cook and a seaman, signs on the stowaway Perce Blackborow once he is found, and writes home. The letter is not the letter of a man selling an expedition. He tells Emily the ship behaves badly against the dock wall in a gale, that she is not as strong as Nimrod, that he would exchange her for the old ship any day now except for comfort. He sails anyway. A century later an engineer reading the wreck will take the same sentence as the first exhibit in the case.
stops.quote: this ship is not as strong as the Nimrod constructionally this I have seen from her way of behaving when in a gale pressing against the dock wall here though there is nothing to be scared of as I think she will go through ice all right only I would exchange her for the old Nimrod any day now except for comfort
stops.quote_source: Shackleton to Emily Shackleton, Buenos Aires, 26 October 1914, Scott Polar Research Institute MS 1537/2/31/6;D, printed in Jukka Tuhkuri, 'Why did Endurance sink?', Polar Record (2025)
suggested_refs: Jukka Tuhkuri, 'Why did Endurance sink?', Polar Record (2025), doi:10.1017/S0032247425100090

stops.name: Grytviken, South Georgia: the last port
stops.date_confidence: attested. Endurance arrived 5 November 1914 and departed 5 December; this stop marks the departure.
stops.campa: Endurance lies a month at the Norwegian whaling station in Cumberland Bay, and the whalers tell Shackleton what he does not want to hear: the ice this season is further north and heavier than any of them remember, and he should wait a year. He does not wait. On the fifth of December she casts off for the Weddell Sea with sixty-nine dogs, a stowaway, a carpenter's cat, and twenty-eight men. None of them will stand on ground that is not ice again for four hundred and ninety-seven days.

stops.name: Weddell Sea, 76 degrees 34 minutes south: beset
stops.date_confidence: sources give 18 or 19 January 1915 for the besetment and the contradiction is left standing (Wikipedia gives 18-19, Britannica 19). The position 76 degrees 34 minutes south, 31 degrees 30 minutes west is attested; chronologies that give latitude -76.34 have read the arc-minutes as a decimal and displace the stop some 25 km north.
stops.campa: Six weeks of working the leads, and then the leads close. At 76 degrees 34 minutes south, within sixty-eight miles of the Vahsel Bay landing where the crossing was to begin, Endurance is frozen fast in a floe that Worsley describes as an almond in a bar of nougat. Shackleton does not tell the crew for some days that they are wintering here. The ship becomes a house that drifts: dog kennels built on the ice, football on the floe, the deck lit through the polar night, and no way off her under her own steam.
suggested_refs: Vahsel Bay, Luitpold Coast (approx. 77.82 south, 35.12 west), the intended landing place for the transcontinental party, never reached

stops.name: Weddell Sea pack ice: all hands onto the ice
stops.date_confidence: attested, position 69 degrees 05 minutes south, 51 degrees 30 minutes west. Ocean Camp was pitched 1 November about a mile and a half from the wreck and is included in this stop; chronologies giving Ocean Camp a position near 30 degrees west are quoting the January besetment longitude instead.
stops.campa: After nine months of drift the pressure comes. Beams buckle, the sternpost is torn away, water gains faster than the pumps can throw it out, and at five in the afternoon Shackleton orders all hands onto the ice. Two days later, before the march begins, he has the carpenter's cat Mrs Chippy and four of the dogs shot on the ground that they cannot contribute to survival; McNish, who owned the cat, never forgives him. The first attempt to haul the boats fails in three days. Ocean Camp is pitched on 1 November within sight of the wreck.
stops.quote: At 5 p.m. I ordered all hands on to the ice. The twisting, grinding floes were working their will at last on the ship.
stops.quote_source: Ernest Shackleton, South (1919), chapter 4, 'Loss of the Endurance'
suggested_refs: Harry McNish's diary, October 1915
Shackleton's own diary, 29 October 1915, on the shooting of Mrs Chippy, Sallie's three youngest pups and Sue's Sirius

stops.name: Weddell Sea: Endurance goes down
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested. The position is Worsley's logged sinking fix, 68 degrees 39 minutes 30 seconds south, 52 degrees 26 minutes 30 seconds west; the wreck was found in 2022 at 68 degrees 44 minutes 21 seconds south, 52 degrees 19 minutes 47 seconds west, 5.4 nautical miles away. Chronologies that place the sinking at the abandonment position are conflating the two.
stops.campa: For twenty-five days the wreck stands in sight of the camp and the men walk back to her for stores and for the ship's log. On the twenty-first of November the stern lifts and Shackleton, watching from the floe, calls out to the others. A crewman's diary entry for that day, which Shackleton copies into his own book without naming the writer, records what they saw: she went down bows first, her stern raised in the air, then one quick dive, and the ice closed over her for ever. In 2022 she is found upright on the seabed three thousand metres down.
suggested_refs: The Endurance22 expedition of the Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust, aboard S.A. Agulhas II, which located the wreck on 5 March 2022 at 3,008 metres; expedition director Mensun Bound. The wreck is a Historic Site and Monument under the Antarctic Treaty System, its protection perimeter widened from 500 to 1,500 metres, with nothing recovered.

stops.name: Patience Camp: the floe splits and the boats go in
stops.date_confidence: the launch date of 9 April 1916 is attested. Patience Camp, occupied from 29 December 1915, was a drifting floe with no fixed position; the coordinates are an approximate placement on the known drift track toward Elephant Island and should not be read as a fix.
stops.campa: Ocean Camp gives way to Patience Camp on the twenty-ninth of December, and Patience Camp drifts north through the winter on a floe that rots steadily under the tents. The remaining dogs are shot, and eaten. On the ninth of April the floe splits between the tents and Shackleton puts three boats into open water: James Caird, Dudley Docker, Stancomb Wills. What follows is seven days of freezing spray, thirst, no sleep, men going out of their minds within earshot of him, and no land under any of them.

segments.name: The Boat Journey and the Crossing of South Georgia

stops.name: Cape Valentine, Elephant Island: the first land in 497 days
stops.date_confidence: the landing is attested; some accounts give 14 or 16 April. Coordinates corrected: Point Wild lies 11 km west of Cape Valentine, so a fix of -61.0333, -54.75 places the cape only 5 km away and too far north. The 497 days are counted from leaving South Georgia on 5 December 1914.
stops.campa: The boats come in under a cliff at the eastern point of Elephant Island and twenty-eight men step onto rock for the first time since December 1914. Some of them cannot stand up on it. One runs shingle through his fingers and lets it fall, and does it again. Blackborow, whose feet are frostbitten past use, is lifted out of the boat and set down in the surf so that he can say he walked ashore. Shackleton sleeps a few hours, looks up at the cliff hanging over the beach, and orders them back into the boats.

stops.name: Point Wild, Elephant Island: the camp under two boats
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eleven kilometres west of the first landing, a low spit of shingle between a glacier and the sea, open to every wind but out of the way of falling rock. No shipping route passes within eight hundred miles of the place, and nobody anywhere in the world knows these men are on it. Frank Wild is left in command of twenty-two of them. The two remaining boats are upended on stones and walled with tent canvas to make a hut, and the men lie inside in a space too low to stand up in, with blubber smoke in it.

stops.name: Point Wild: the James Caird sails for South Georgia
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eight hundred nautical miles of the worst water on the planet lie between the beach and the whaling stations, and Worsley will get four sun sights in seventeen days to cross it by. Six men go: Shackleton, Worsley to navigate, Crean, McNish, McCarthy and Vincent. They carry four weeks of food, because Shackleton reasons that if they have not reached South Georgia in four weeks they will not reach it at all. McNish has decked the boat over with sledge runners, packing-case lids, and canvas thawed soft over a blubber stove.
suggested_refs: The James Caird itself, preserved at Dulwich College; replicas James Caird II (2000, Hamburg), James Caird III (2008, South Georgia Museum) and Alexandra Shackleton (2012), the last used by Tim Jarvis to re-create the voyage and the island crossing in 2013

stops.name: King Haakon Bay, South Georgia: the wrong side of the island
stops.date_confidence: attested. South Georgia was sighted on 8 May and the landing made on 10 May after two days unable to close the coast in a hurricane.
stops.campa: They raise South Georgia on the eighth of May and cannot land. A hurricane holds them off the coast for two days, the same storm that sinks a five-hundred-ton steamer bound for the island. On the tenth they get in through a gap in the reef at the mouth of King Haakon Bay, on the uninhabited side, with the whaling stations on the far coast and the boat no longer fit to go round. The first thing they do ashore is drink from a stream running off the glacier. They have been rationing water for six days.

stops.name: Peggotty Camp, King Haakon Bay: the boat turned over for a roof
stops.date_confidence: the party moved to the head of the bay in mid-May and left on 19 May; the exact day of the move is not fixed and defaults to 15 May. Coordinates corrected to Peggotty Bluff at the head of the bay, from a fix that placed the camp some 25 km inland among the mountains.
stops.campa: At the head of the bay they haul the boat up, turn her over and live under her. Shackleton names the place Peggotty Camp, after the family in David Copperfield who kept house in an upturned boat on the sand at Yarmouth. McNish, McCarthy and Vincent stay here: McNish and Vincent are finished, and McCarthy is left to look after them. The three who go are Shackleton, Worsley and Crean, with fifty feet of rope, a carpenter's adze for an ice axe, and screws taken out of the boat driven through their boot soles for grip.
suggested_refs: Charles Dickens, David Copperfield, for the Peggotty boat-house on the Yarmouth sands

stops.name: South Georgia interior: thirty-six hours across an unmapped island
stops.date_confidence: the crossing is attested at roughly 36 hours, 19 to 20 May 1916. This point is an approximate midpoint of a route that was never surveyed, for which no map existed, and should not be read as a documented waypoint.
stops.campa: No one has crossed the interior of South Georgia and there is no map of it. They start at three in the morning by moonlight, climb to a ridge four times and are turned back three, and at the fourth gap, with darkness and frost coming down and no way off the ice, they coil the rope into a pad, sit on it, and slide the mountain in the dark. They do not stop for thirty-six hours. Afterwards each of the three tells the others, separately, that a fourth man had been walking with them, and none of them can account for it.
stops.quote: I know that during that long and racking march of thirty-six hours over the unnamed mountains and glaciers of South Georgia it seemed to me often that we were four, not three.
stops.quote_source: Ernest Shackleton, South (1919), chapter 10, 'Across South Georgia'
suggested_refs: Frank Worsley's remark to Shackleton, quoted in South, chapter 10: 'Boss, I had a curious feeling on the march that there was another person with us.' The episode is the origin of the phrase the Third Man Factor.

stops.name: Stromness whaling station: the manager does not recognise him
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They come down the last slope through a waterfall and walk into the station: three men in rags, hair to their shoulders, unwashed for a year. Two boys run away from them. Thoralf Sorlle, the manager, who entertained Shackleton at his own table eighteen months before, stands in his doorway and does not know him. Shackleton says who he is and asks when the war ended. It has not ended. That night a whaleboat goes round the coast for the three men left at King Haakon Bay.
stops.quote: No other civilized men could have been as blankly ignorant of world-shaking happenings as we were when we reached Stromness Whaling Station.

stops.name: Punta Arenas: the borrowed ships
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period June-August 1916; the relief attempts were mounted from Port Stanley, Montevideo and Punta Arenas, and this stop stands for the whole campaign. The day defaults to the first of June.
stops.campa: Three times Shackleton takes a ship south for Elephant Island and three times the pack turns him back: the Southern Sky out of Port Stanley, the Uruguayan trawler Instituto de Pesca No. 1, the schooner Emma out of Punta Arenas. He is not sleeping. The Admiralty tells him no relief vessel can be spared before October, and October will be too late. The British community of Punta Arenas raises the money for one attempt themselves. In the end the Chilean government lends him a small steel-hulled tug with no heating and no searchlight.

stops.name: Point Wild: the Yelcho comes in
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Yelcho comes through open water on the fourth attempt with Luis Pardo commanding, and Shackleton stands in the bow counting the figures coming down the shingle. Worsley hears him counting. At twenty-two he sits down. The men have lived four and a half months under two upturned boats on limpets and penguin, Frank Wild rolling up his sleeping bag each morning with the words that the Boss may come today. They are aboard within an hour. All twenty-eight of the Weddell Sea party are alive.
suggested_refs: Luis Pardo and the Chilean naval tug Yelcho, 30 August 1916

stops.name: Cape Evans, Ross Island: the other half of the expedition
stops.date_confidence: the repaired Aurora's arrival is attested to 10 January 1917. Shackleton sailed with her, after a public dispute over what his role in the relief should be; the coordinates are those of Cape Evans, where the stranded party had wintered.
stops.campa: The other half of the expedition has spent two years laying depots across the Ross Ice Shelf for a crossing that never began. Their ship was wrenched from her moorings by a gale in May 1915 and carried out to sea, leaving ten men ashore with almost no supplies. They laid the depots anyway. Arnold Spencer-Smith died on the Barrier of scurvy; Aeneas Mackintosh and Victor Hayward walked out onto rotten sea ice in May 1916 and were never seen again. Shackleton comes ashore with the relief on 10 January 1917 and takes off the seven who are left.

segments.name: The War, the Book, and the Last Ship

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the propaganda mission
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period October 1917 into 1918; the month of arrival is not fixed in reachable sources and the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Too old for the trenches and refused a command, Shackleton is sent to South America by the British government to talk Argentina and Chile toward the Allied side. He lectures, dines, works the British communities and reports back that the job is not going well. He has been home in England barely four months when he takes the posting, and it carries him back into the port Endurance sailed from in 1914. Almost nothing of the mission survives in his own hand, and what is known of the eight months comes secondhand. He is drinking.
sources: dossier synthesis of the 1917-1918 South American mission

stops.name: Tromso, Norway: the collapse on the way to Spitsbergen
stops.date_confidence: attested to spring 1918; the exact dates of the Spitsbergen venture are not fixed in reachable sources and the day defaults to the first of April. The account of the illness rests on secondary biography rather than a medical record.
stops.campa: Sent north to look at a Spitsbergen mining and strategic scheme, Shackleton gets as far as the Arctic town of Tromso and collapses. A heart attack is suspected and a doctor is brought, but he will not be examined; he never is. He is forty-four. What happened at Tromso reaches the record through his biographers and not through any medical note, so the nature of the illness is not known. He leaves the venture, and in July he is appointed instead to the North Russian expeditionary force.
sources: dossier synthesis of the Spitsbergen venture

stops.name: Murmansk: temporary major, North Russia
stops.date_confidence: the appointment as temporary major is attested to 22 July 1918 and the service to the period October 1918 to March 1919, spanning Murmansk and Archangel; the day defaults to the first of October. The Scott Polar Research Institute holds his North Russia notebook, 1918-1919.
stops.campa: Major Shackleton, temporary, of the British Army, arrives at Murmansk to advise on winter equipment for the Allied intervention in the Russian Civil War. He works up a sledging ration and a windproof jerkin, and the jerkin is issued and named after him. Around him gather the men from the ice again: Worsley, Macklin, Hussey, Stenhouse, on the Archangel front through the winter. He also floats a scheme for the mineral resources of the Kola peninsula, which dies when the intervention does. He is made OBE in the Military Division in 1919.
suggested_refs: Scott Polar Research Institute, 'North Russia notebook, 1918-1919'
sources: Scott Polar Research Institute archival holding (via dossier)

stops.name: London: South goes to the printer
stops.date_confidence: the book was published by William Heinemann in 1919, with a second edition in December; the stop is dated to that December edition and the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Shackleton dictates the Endurance book to the New Zealand journalist Edward Saunders, as he had dictated the Nimrod book to the same man ten years earlier, and Leonard Hussey edits it without payment. Half of it is not his own: the Ross Sea party chapters are assembled from other men's diaries. It sells, but not enough. He follows it with a season at the Philharmonic Hall, twice a day, standing in front of a screen of Frank Hurley's photographs and telling the story to a country that has just buried three quarters of a million men.
stops.quote: After the conquest of the South Pole by Amundsen, who, by a narrow margin of days only, was in advance of the British Expedition under Scott, there remained but one great main object of Antarctic journeyings, the crossing of the South Polar continent from sea to sea.
stops.quote_source: Ernest Shackleton, South: The Story of Shackleton's Last Expedition 1914-1917 (1919), Preface (punctuation of the original dash rendered as a comma)
suggested_refs: South is in the public domain and is available in full via Wikisource, Project Gutenberg (ebook 5199) and Standard Ebooks

stops.name: St Katharine Docks, London: the Quest and the old crew
stops.date_confidence: Quest left St Katharine Docks on 17 September 1921, after inspection by King George V, and left Plymouth on 24 September; chronologies that treat 17 and 24 September as rival dates for one departure are conflating two separate ones.
stops.campa: Quest is a small Norwegian sealer, slow and underpowered, bought with money from John Quiller Rowett, a schoolfellow from Dulwich. The programme changes several times: an Arctic expedition, then oceanography, then a loose plan to circumnavigate Antarctica with a seaplane and survey islands nobody has landed on. What does not change is the crew. Wild, Worsley, Macklin, McIlroy, Hussey, Green, Kerr and McLeod all sign on again, most of them for less than they could earn ashore.

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the attack he refuses to have examined
stops.date_confidence: Quest reached Rio on 22 November 1921 and lay there four weeks for an engine overhaul and a new topmast; the suspected heart attack is dated 17 December. Chronologies placing the attack in November are dating it to the arrival instead.
stops.campa: The engines fail on the way south and Quest lies a month at Rio while they are stripped. He has collapsed before, at Tromso and on the Discovery southern journey, and has never once let a doctor listen properly to his chest. A paper published in 2016 will propose, working backward from the accounts, a hole in the heart he was born with. On the seventeenth of December Shackleton has what Macklin believes is a heart attack. He will not be examined. In the morning he says he is better, and the subject closes.
suggested_refs: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine (2016), proposing retrospectively an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with episodic dysrhythmia, superimposed on later coronary disease. A hypothesis about a man dead ninety-four years, not a lifetime diagnosis.
sources: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine (2016), via dossier

stops.name: Grytviken: death aboard the Quest
stops.date_confidence: arrival on 4 January and death in the small hours of 5 January are attested; sources give the time as shortly after 02:00 or as about 02:50, and the discrepancy is left standing. The exchange with Macklin is reported from Macklin's own account as printed by Margery and James Fisher (1957), pp. 476-478, not from the original notebook; the widely quoted paraphrase 'What do you want me to give up now?' is not the attested wording.
stops.campa: Quest anchors off Grytviken on the fourth of January, eight years after Endurance last lay in this bay. Shackleton writes in his diary that night about a lone star hovering gem-like above the harbour. In the small hours he calls Macklin to his cabin with back pain, and Macklin tells him he has been overdoing things and ought to lead a more regular life. Shackleton asks what it is he ought to give up. Chiefly alcohol, Boss, Macklin says. Minutes later the attack comes, and he is dead at forty-seven.
stops.quote: You are always wanting me to give up things, what is it I ought to give up?
stops.quote_source: Shackleton to Alexander Macklin aboard Quest at Grytviken, 5 January 1922, in Margery and James Fisher, Shackleton (1957), pp. 476-478
suggested_refs: Macklin's finding, recorded at the time: atheroma of the coronary arteries and heart failure

stops.name: Grytviken cemetery: buried among the whalers
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The body goes north toward England and gets as far as Montevideo, where a cable from Emily turns it around: bury him in the south. He comes back to Grytviken and is put in the whalers' cemetery on the fifth of March, among Norwegian sailors, after a short Lutheran service read by Edward Binnie, with the fleet's flags at half mast. The grave faces south. Frank Wild takes the Quest on south without him. Macklin writes that the place is fitting, standing lonely on an island far from civilization, surrounded by a stormy tempestuous sea.
suggested_refs: Robert Browning, 'The Statue and the Bust': 'Let a man contend to the uttermost / For his life's set prize, be it what it will!' These lines, used as the epigraph of Mill's 1923 authorised biography, are the Browning long associated with the grave; the wording usually quoted as the inscription, 'I hold that a man should strive to the uttermost for his life's set prize,' is not Browning's text and could not be verified in any reachable source. Frank Wild, in Shackleton's Last Voyage, records a different Browning at the memorial cairn, from 'A Grammarian's Funeral'.
The ashes of Frank Wild were interred beside the grave on 27 November 2011, the headstone reading 'Frank Wild 1873-1939, Shackleton's right-hand man'.
sources: Hugh Robert Mill, The Life of Sir Ernest Shackleton (1923)
